title: NFL Week 4 Preview: Tony Romo FIRED; Are Browns for Real? Is Travis Kelce on Tight End Mount Rushmore? Plus, Best Bets & Fantasy sleeper starts

title: Jeff Legwold joins Kreckman and Lindahl 10-2-26
text: Every Bud Light Football Friday, we talk to Jeff Legwald here on the Kreckman and Lindahl Show. And we get you all set for the Bronco weekend. That will be Denver at San Francisco on Sunday afternoon. Jeff Legwald of ESPN is with us as he always is. Jeff, I choose to begin this interview by asking a question posed in a headline story. written by Jeff Legwald on ESPN.com. Jeff, I ask you, can the Broncos keep pulling off unlikely comeback victories? Well, they certainly keep providing more information on their side of the equation at the moment than the, this can't work over the long haul. And I think, you know, they are the analytical outlier for, and all of this, you know, Sunday was the 13th one score win the team has had since the start of last season. And that, that is just a ridiculous number in any way you frame it. And, you know, everybody I know in the league who has any sort of part in an analytical department will always talk about regression to the mean and, you know, all of, all of these things. And, in terms of comeback wins and one score victories, they haven't hit the wall yet. But I think the head coach certainly is, you know, he always has a hint of pessimism anyway, but I think he would rather not walk the tightrope so often. But I think if they somehow find a way to keep the defense playing On the key downs, the way they played, you know, in the second half of these games that they've won, and Bo Nix can sort of be the guy who steers the car just well enough at the end, it is a formula right now, and it is working. And I think there is something to be said. You know, however many points it's worth, they truly believe they can function well in that environment. And I think that's the real tangible bonus and all this that I've been around a lot of teams that wondered how they would do, you know, when the pressure was on and they wondered how they would do if they were down to the last down, you know, in, in the game. And this team doesn't wonder they know, and that can be a little bit of a powerful advantage. Well, there's no doubt about it, Jeff. Here's the thing. I keep relating to the mid-80s Broncos because that's just what a lot of this feels like at times with the magical comebacks and all this. But you also know in the Super Bowls or in some of the bigger games, all of a sudden you don't keep the game in check. You don't keep everybody in distance. You don't keep them in a space and they reel them in. And I guess that's what everybody's worried about. And also, you know, we always ask you every week, can you explain why it looks one way in the first half and another way in the second? You keep pointing to the run game. Nate has talked about how bad this Niners run defense has been, at least by the numbers. Is this the true test this week where if they don't get it figured out, we should be concerned? Well, I always think that. I think they're willing to be more true to the team they are when the heat's on. You know, it's easy at the beginning of the game to say, having spent this week game planning and you get all these great ideas about what you want to do. And I think sometimes, and, you know, I think Davis, Davis wedge, a first year play caller, sometimes you call the game. You sort of always wanted to call instead of the one for the team in front of you. And I think they're more apt to do that. You know, whether it's Sean Payton or, scowling down at him, you know, with the, I better see some run, some runs here on the next possession or, or just the, the nature of the game, you know, you're behind, things are going poorly. You, you move toward what you're good at. And I think if they would do that sooner, it would look better. But you know, that old, principle or the solution might be the most simple one is sometimes hard to get to. Jeff Legwald brought to you by the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, IBEW Local 68. You start with a job, you end with a career. You know, Jeff, it feels as though we wring hands over the Broncos offense every single week, but let's go looking at the other side right now because this is the heavyweight matchup that everybody wants to see. Kyle Shanahan and this Niners offense going up against Vijay and this Broncos defense. As you look at this matchup, Jeff, of the best offense in the league against, and we know how good Denver's defense is, where does San Francisco have the advantages? Where does Denver have the advantages as they go head-to-head? Yeah, I mean, I think knowing the people involved with the 49ers, the they're going to come after the Bronco linebackers, you know, whether that's with Kittle, McCaffrey, you know, Debo, you know, however they do it, I would guess they're looking to isolate Bronco linebackers in coverage. So I would expect the Broncos in some way to try to respond with, with maybe a big nickel formation. You know, I I'm, I'm certain they may toss out a, a, a, I'm not certain, but knowing everybody and how they call things, I would expect to see a 4-4 at times on defense, which they haven't used too many snaps this year because you just got to muscle up against the 49ers and somehow keep enough speed on the field to deal with what they have because that's where they challenge you. They try to put your bigger people in bad spots and are very good at doing it. And I think that's their advantage because that's been a trouble spot for the Broncos. And, you know, Kittle has done plenty of damage, you know, including the 200-yard receiving game, you know, when DJ was the head coach. So that's their advantage. But the Broncos will be the first team that truly pressures Brock Purdy. they've gotten not a free pass because I do not want to cheapen how Purdy is playing. He's at an MVP level. And I think this notion of, can we just stop arguing about whether he's a good quarterback or not? The guy is a really good quarterback. He's playing better than any other quarterback in the league right now, say for Josh Allen, maybe in Lamar. But that's the company he's in. Let's just get over the fact he was late in the draft and move on. But that said, I've looked at the Niners games this year, and I've charted them, and he has remained clean. He's not been sacked because he's not been pressured even very often. And I think that will be a difference. And the Niners offense will have to respond to that. They're going to have to leave more people in than they want to And that removes somebody from the pattern. So, I mean, I think that's the chess match I would be watching is how often do the 49ers have to leave extra people in and how often do the Broncos have to rush extra people? Because those are going to be the downs that probably matter. Jeff, you talked about Brock Purdy right there. And, you know, you go way back with Kyle Shanahan. Why has Brock Purdy... been the perfect Kyle Shanahan quarterback? Part of it is Kyle, like his dad, knew what he wanted in a quarterback. It's not some mystical skill set he's looking for. It's a very defined profile that they're looking for. I think sometimes in the public domain before the draft, people look at quarterbacks from the arm end and That's just not how to do it. I know it's entertaining. And I know those throws at pro day with no defense on the field anywhere, you know, are just amazing to people. And sometimes they are amazing, but it doesn't have a lot to do with how you play quarterback. And, you know, he's looking for processors, guys who can sift through the information and Find the right people and throw a tight window throw. Because if you can't throw in a tight window in the NFL, people are always going to ask you why you haven't lived up to your draft standing or whatever. Because that is everything. Accuracy is everything. And he leads the league by a fairly wide margin right now in least off-target attempts this year. He puts the ball... where it belongs. He's at like 4%, which is ridiculous. I think that number is right. I don't have it right in front of me, but i uh he's he's several percentage points ahead of the next person and that's that's really a a metric that you should pay attention to because that's what matters are you putting the ball on target and he does better than anybody right now and that's why he hasn't been sacked and that's why he leads the league and and uh you know, all of the passing metrics people care about for the most part, the second and completion percentage. So, but that's, that's, that's why he fits because he can work through the equation quickly and get to the right answer in real time. And he recognizes pressure before the snap and the best quarterbacks, find the pressure, even disguised, you know, before the snap and the ones who struggle do not. And he's got all of those traits. All right. It's funny because it's not my question, but they're just pointing out NFL live. Brock Purdy's got the best QBR through three games since 2006. And that include guys like Josh Allen and Peyton Manning in the run in those games. So he's playing as well. As you thought. Okay. So an interesting comparison between, that we had on the station from Niners Radio out there in the Bay Area, Jeff, where the analysts were saying, the talk shows were talking about how Brock Purdy, and this goes to some of what you talked about, learned how to play quarterback first and is using some of his athleticism now. They said they think Bo Nix has been using his athleticism first and now needs to learn better how to play quarterback. Would you agree with that assessment? What would that mean in your mind for Bo as far as progression? You know, Andy, I think that's always the case for– any quarterback who moves from college to the NFL who had any kind of mobility, they lean on it often because they can. And the level of mobility to be considered successfully mobile in college, the bar is far lower than it is in the NFL. So you have more guys leading on that crutch than they should when they come to the league because they've gotten away with it. The other issue is a tight window in college is like a three-yard opening. And a tight window in the NFL is basically the distance from your elbow to the tip of your middle finger. That's open in the NFL in a tight window situation. And those are the ones where the development comes. And Bo's tight window metrics aren't spectacular. And he's still working against how it looks against pressure and all of those things. But he's in the third year and he was thrown in the deep end immediately. So you can't deny the winning percentage for Bo, but he's He's not as advanced in processing the information and what it all looks like than some other guys in the league. And that is, like any guy going through his fourth, fifth, sixth years as a starter, as Nick's will, that's their hurdle is remembering all the information you've already gathered. You've already faced. You face some of these coordinators. You face some of these teams. You face some of these defenses. You know, what did you take away and what can you apply in the future? Hey, Jeff, one more thing before we get you out of here. It's funny. You covered Mike Shanahan forever and his kid is 3-0. You covered Gary Kubiak forever and his kid is 3-0. What is Clint Kubiak doing right now with these Raiders, and what is sustainable over the long haul when their schedule heats up, especially this week against Kansas City?
